16	
17	# LaTeX 论文写作全流程
18	
19	ML/AI 顶会论文从草稿到投稿的完整指南。整合 Orchestra Research、VibeSkills、claim2evidence 三方最佳实践。
20	
21	---
22	
23	## 1. 工作模式
24	
25	开始前选择模式：
26	
27	| 模式 | 说明 | 适用 |
28	|------|------|------|
29	| **Build** | 从实验笔记/结果/代码生成论文 | 新稿 |
30	| **Improve** | 改写已有章节，强化论证 | 修改稿 |
31	| **Audit** | 输出风险列表 + 缺失证据 + 修复建议 | 投前检查 |
32	
33	---
34	
35	## 2. Claim-Evidence 方法论
36	
37	**核心原则：论文是一个有中心贡献的故事，不是实验的堆砌。**
38	
39	### 2.1 一句话贡献
40	
41	在写任何内容之前，必须能用一句话说清贡献。如果不能，说明还没准备好写论文。
42	
43	### 2.2 Claim-Evidence Map
44	
45	为每个 contribution 建立 claim→evidence 映射表：
46	
47	| Contribution | Claim | Evidence | Table/Figure |
48	|-------------|-------|----------|-------------|
49	| C1: 方法 X 在 Y 上 SOTA | 比所有 baseline 高 ≥2% | 5-seed 平均，p<0.05 | Table 1 |
50	| C2: 消融证明 Z 是关键 | 去掉 Z 后掉 >5% | 消融实验 | Table 2 |
51	| C3: 计算效率 | 比 baseline 快 3× | FLOPs + wall-clock | Figure 3 |
52	
53	**没有直接证据支撑的 claim 必须删除或降级为 discussion。**
54	
55	### 2.3 章节起草顺序
56	
57	```
58	1. Introduction + Experiments（先确定 claim 和 evidence）
59	2. Method（评估问题稳定后再写细节）
60	3. Related Work
61	4. Abstract + Title（核心 claim 定型后最后写）
62	```
63	
64	### 2.4 Quality Gates
65	
66	投稿前必须通过：
67	- [ ] 前两段出现显式 novelty 声明
68	- [ ] 每个 contribution 有可验证的 evidence
69	- [ ] Abstract / Intro / Conclusion 的 claim 一致
70	- [ ] Limitations 真实且技术性诚实
71	- [ ] 审稿人两分钟内能识别 delta
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 3. 引用防幻觉（CRITICAL）
76	
77	**AI 生成引用有 ~40% 错误率。绝对禁止凭记忆写 BibTeX。**
78	
79	### 3.1 黄金法则
80	
81	```
82	IF 无法程序化获取引用:
83	    → 标记 [CITATION NEEDED] 或 \cite{PLACEHOLDER_verify}
84	    → 明确告知用户
85	    → 绝不编造看似合理的引用
86	```
87	
88	### 3.2 五步验证流程
89	
90	```
91	1. SEARCH  → Semantic Scholar API 搜索关键词
92	2. VERIFY  → 至少 2 个来源确认论文存在（S2 + arXiv/CrossRef）
93	3. RETRIEVE → 通过 DOI 获取 BibTeX（程序化，非记忆）
94	4. CHECK   → 确认

2	name: paper-writing-norms
3	description: 顶会级别论文写作风格规范——章节写法（Abstract/Intro/Related Work）、去 AI 风格、视觉密度、叙事哲学。Paper Agent 和 Worker 写论文章节时必须加载。
4	allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep]
5	scope: global
6	version: 2
7	priority: 9
8	tags:
9	  - writing
10	  - paper
11	  - style
12	  - norms
13	roles:
14	  - agent
15	  - worker
16	  - paper_agent
17	---
18	
19	# 论文写作风格规范
20	
21	> 核心哲学：**论文是一个有说服力的故事，不是实验报告。** 审稿人在几十秒内判断论文价值——如果 Abstract 和 Introduction 读起来像实验日志，论文就已经失败了。
22	
23	---
24	
25	## 一、总体写作哲学
26	
27	### 1.1 故事驱动，不是数据堆砌
28	
29	- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证
30	- 禁止大量实验数据堆砌——每个数字出现必须服务于叙事推进
31	- 附录内容必须在正文中有明确引用且融入叙事，禁止简单堆砌
32	- 如果附录数据对核心叙事有重大影响，根据附录数据调整论文 framing
33	
34	### 1.2 主线统一性
35	
36	- 当 idea 在研究过程中发生变化后，**必须重审全文逻辑**
37	- 常见问题：Introduction 讲的故事 A，Method 做的是故事 B，Results 又在讲故事 C
38	- 修复方式：从最终实验结论反推，重写 Introduction 的问题定义和动机
39	- 每次 idea 调整后检查：Abstract → Introduction → Method → Results → Discussion → Conclusion 是否形成一条连贯主线
40	
41	### 1.3 专有名词必须有定义
42	
43	- 首次出现的专有名词/缩写必须给出完整定义和解释
44	- Abstract 中使用的缩写也必须在 Abstract 内定义（如 LLM = Large Language Model）
45	- 不能假设读者知道你自己定义的术语——论文从来没解释过的概念不能直接使用
46	- 通用规则：如果一个非标准术语第一次出现时没有括号定义，就是写作 bug
47	
48	### 1.4 写作前必读同类优秀论文
49	
50	- 每个章节动笔前，找 **2-3 篇目标会议近 1-2 年的高分论文**作为风格参考——同类问题或同类方法皆可
51	- 重点学：
52	  - Abstract 怎么用最少篇幅讲完故事
53	  - Introduction 怎么从大问题切入到具体贡献
54	  - Related Work 怎么 positioning 自己（不是 survey）
55	  - Table/Figure 怎么压缩信息密度
56	- **不是抄袭**，是学习同行的故事节奏和审美——不同子领域叙事节奏差异很大
57	- 实操：Paper Agent 可以从 `literature_map.yaml` 中挑 `role=foundation` 或 `role=direct-competitor` 的论文，把 `{title, venue, year, abstract}` 附在 Worker 的 task_prompt 中作为概念参考；如需学习写作风格本身，让 Worker 通过 WebSearch 取得论文链接并 fetch 全文
58	
59	---
60	
61	## 二、Abstract 写作规范
62	
63	### 2.1 四个必答问题（150-250 words）
64	
65	Abstract 必须在很短的篇幅内清楚回答：
66	1. **研究什么问题** — 1-2 句话交代背景和痛点
67	2. **为什么重要** — 现有方法的不足（不用写太多）
68	3. **本文提出什么** — 核心贡献的关键机制（简要，不堆砌细节）
69	4. **结果说明什么** — 用具体实验结论支撑贡献
70	
71	### 2.2 禁忌
72	
73	- **禁止堆砌数据**：Abstract 不是 Results 的缩写。最多引用 2-3 个关键数字，要服务于 claim
74	- **

7	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
8	\label{sec:setup}
9	
10	\paragraph{Datasets.}
11	We train on 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak conversations and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, both generated via Qwen3-8B.
12	Topic anchoring ensures that benign conversations cover the same subject domains as jailbreak conversations and controls for topical confounds.
13	For out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, we generate 80 Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024} and 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} conversations through a separate pipeline with no overlap in attack templates or strategies with the training data.
14	The in-distribution (IID) test set consists of 76 held-out Crescendo conversations (38 jailbreak, 38 benign).
15	To assess adversarial robustness, we paraphrase the IID test set to produce 76 perturbed samples with mean BERTScore of 0.92 and lexical overlap of 0.20, confirming that surface forms change substantially while semantics are preserved.
16	
17	\paragraph{Baselines.}
18	We compare three detection methods.

% introduction.tex — DisPeD Introduction Section

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a qualitatively different threat to large language model (LLM) safety than their single-turn counterparts. Attacks such as Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo}, Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024}, and Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} achieve high attack success rates by distributing adversarial intent across a sequence of individually benign turns. No single turn contains an explicit harmful request; instead, the attacker gradually steers the conversation toward a forbidden goal through rapport building, logical reframing, and incremental escalation. Representation engineering analyses confirm that individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as genuinely benign text in pretrained encoders~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}, rendering per-turn safety filters ineffective. The common mechanism underlying these attacks is \emph{persuasion}: each attack type implements a distinct but systematic strategy for manipulating the model's compliance over multiple conversational exchanges~\citep{li2024mhj}. Detecting these attacks therefore requires moving beyond content-level analysis to capture the pragmatic dynamics of the conversation.

Current defenses fail to address this challenge. Production safety classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and cannot model manipulation trajectories that unfold across multiple exchanges. The natural alternative is to encode full conversations with a pretrained language model and track semantic drift over turns. This approach, exemplified by temporal aggregation over generic embeddings (the ``DeepContext'' paradigm~\citep{deepcontext2026}), performs well when the test distribution matches training: all methods we evaluate, including bag-of-words baselines, achieve near-perfect F1 on in-distribution Crescendo conversations. The critical failure emerges on unseen attack types. A vanilla DeBERTa encoder with the same temporal aggregation pipeline collapses from F1 = 1.000 on in-distribution data to F1 = 0.284 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight conversations. This collapse worsens as more turns are observed (F1 drops from 0.575 at turn 1 to 0.284 on the full conversation), consistent with the finding that each additional attack turn supplies misleading ``benign'' evidence to the generic encoder~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}. LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 achieves F1 of only 0.191 to 0.449 on Crescendo detection, with 30 to 47\% of responses unparseable, confirming that content-level reasoning cannot detect adversarial intent distributed across benign turns. The gap is clear: existing methods either ignore multi-turn structure entirely or rely on representations that fail to generalize across attack families.

The key observation motivating our approach is that persuasion in jailbreak attacks is both \emph{systematic} and \emph{extractable}. \citet{zeng2024pap} identify 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak attacks through their Persuasion Attack Paradigm, and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} find identifiable persuasion strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. Recent work on LLM persuasion demonstrates that these pragmatic dynamics leave detectable traces in turn-level representations~\citep{jaipersaud2025howdollmspersuade}. If persuasion is systematic (attacks follow identifiable strategy patterns) and extractable (representations can encode these patterns), then fine-tuning an encoder on persuasion-related text should teach it to attend to pragmatic features rather than topical content. The resulting representations would capture the functional structure of manipulation, a structure shared across attack types regardless of their surface realization. This is not a new theoretical claim but an operationalization of observations already established in the literature: our contribution is to demonstrate that this operationalization produces measurable gains in cross-attack generalization.

We propose \textbf{DisPeD} (Discourse-level Persuasion Detection), a two-stage framework that implements this idea. In Stage~1, we fine-tune a DeBERTa-v3-base encoder~\citep{he2021deberta} with a multi-task objective that combines 8-class persuasion strategy classification and binary jailbreak-intent classification at the turn level. The 8-class taxonomy is grounded in the Persuasion Attack Paradigm~\citep{zeng2024pap} and Cialdini's principles of influence~\citep{cialdini2001influence}, covering strategies from rapport building and authority appeal to gradual escalation and direct request. The persuasion classification task forces the encoder to learn representations that distinguish between pragmatic strategies, while the intent task anchors these representations to the detection objective. In Stage~2, we aggregate turn-level [CLS] embeddings via mean pooling and train a lightweight MLP for conversation-level binary classification. The full architecture is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}. The design is deliberately simple: the ablation study (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that replacing mean pooling with a GRU yields no improvement, and that even scrambled persuasion labels reduce OOD detection by only 1 percentage point (pp) relative to the full taxonomy, while vanilla DeBERTa without fine-tuning trails by over 70~pp. The fine-tuning process on persuasion-related text, not label accuracy or temporal modeling, is the critical ingredient for cross-attack generalization.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Cross-attack generalization through persuasion-aware fine-tuning.} DisPeD achieves F1 = 1.000 on unseen Deceptive Delight conversations, a +72~pp improvement over vanilla DeBERTa (F1 = 0.284) trained on the same Crescendo data. Ablation experiments show that scrambled strategy labels reduce OOD F1 by only 1~pp, confirming that fine-tuning on persuasion-domain text is the mechanism that bridges the cross-attack generalization gap (Section~\ref{sec:cross_attack}, Section~\ref{sec:ablation}).

  \item \textbf{Interpretable detection through persuasion strategy trajectories.} The 8-class persuasion taxonomy provides native interpretability: different attack types exhibit distinct strategy signatures that security analysts can inspect. Crescendo uses all 8 strategies with gradual escalation across turns; FITD employs only 4 strategies in a commitment-then-escalation pattern. These trajectories explain detection decisions without requiring post-hoc interpretability methods (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).

  \item \textbf{Robustness to adversarial perturbation.} DisPeD maintains zero degradation (0~pp) under adversarial paraphrasing, while vanilla DeBERTa degrades by 11.8~pp and TF-IDF by 1.3~pp. Combined with cross-attack robustness, this confirms that persuasion-aware representations are invariant to both surface variation and attack-type shift (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
\end{itemize}

% introduction.tex -- DisPeD Introduction Section

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a qualitatively different threat to large language model (LLM) safety than their single-turn counterparts. Attacks such as Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo}, Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024}, and Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} achieve high attack success rates by distributing adversarial intent across a sequence of individually benign turns. No single turn contains an explicit harmful request; instead, the attacker gradually steers the conversation toward a forbidden goal through rapport building, logical reframing, and incremental escalation. A Crescendo attacker, for instance, might begin with a factual question about historical chemistry, follow up with a request for ``educational'' synthesis procedures, and only in the final turn request instructions for producing a controlled substance. Each intermediate turn is indistinguishable from a legitimate query. Representation engineering analyses confirm that individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as genuinely benign text in pretrained encoders~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}, rendering per-turn safety filters ineffective. The common mechanism underlying these attacks is \emph{persuasion}: each attack type implements a distinct but systematic strategy for manipulating the model's compliance over multiple conversational exchanges~\citep{li2024mhj}. Detecting these attacks therefore requires moving beyond content-level analysis to capture the pragmatic dynamics of the conversation.

Current defenses fail to address this challenge along two axes: granularity and representation. Production safety classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and cannot model manipulation trajectories that unfold across multiple exchanges. These systems are designed to detect overtly harmful content in isolation and are fundamentally blind to the distributed nature of multi-turn attacks, where the adversarial intent only becomes apparent through the cumulative progression of turns. The natural alternative is to encode full conversations with a pretrained language model and track semantic drift over turns. This approach, exemplified by temporal aggregation over generic embeddings (the ``DeepContext'' paradigm~\citep{deepcontext2026}), performs well when the test distribution matches training: all methods we evaluate, including bag-of-words baselines, achieve near-perfect F1 on in-distribution Crescendo conversations. The critical failure emerges on unseen attack types. A vanilla DeBERTa encoder with the same temporal aggregation pipeline collapses from F1 = 1.000 on in-distribution data to F1 = 0.284 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight conversations. This collapse worsens as more turns are observed (F1 drops from 0.575 at turn 1 to 0.284 on the full conversation), consistent with the finding that each additional attack turn supplies misleading ``benign'' evidence to the generic encoder~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}. LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 achieves F1 of only 0.191 to 0.449 on Crescendo detection, with 30 to 47\% of responses unparseable, confirming that content-level reasoning cannot detect adversarial intent distributed across benign turns. The gap is clear: no existing method uses persuasion-grounded representations, and methods that rely on surface semantics or content-level reasoning fail to generalize across attack families.

The key observation motivating our approach is that persuasion in jailbreak attacks is both \emph{systematic} and \emph{extractable}. \citet{zeng2024pap} identify 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak attacks through their Persuasion Attack Paradigm (PAP), and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} find identifiable persuasion strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. These findings establish that multi-turn attacks are not ad hoc manipulation but structured persuasion campaigns that follow recognizable patterns. On the extraction side, recent work on LLM persuasion demonstrates that these pragmatic dynamics leave detectable traces in turn-level representations~\citep{jaipersaud2025howdollmspersuade}, and that the persuasion literature offers well-established taxonomies (e.g., Cialdini's six principles of influence~\citep{cialdini2001influence}) to categorize these strategies. If persuasion is systematic (attacks follow identifiable strategy patterns) and extractable (representations can encode these patterns), then fine-tuning an encoder on persuasion-related text should teach it to attend to pragmatic features rather than topical content. The resulting representations would capture the functional structure of manipulation, a structure shared across attack types regardless of their surface realization. This is not a new theoretical claim but an operationalization of observations already established in the literature: our contribution is to demonstrate that this operationalization produces measurable gains in cross-attack generalization.

We propose \textbf{DisPeD} (Discourse-level Persuasion Detection), a two-stage framework that implements this idea. In Stage~1, we fine-tune a DeBERTa-v3-base encoder~\citep{he2021deberta} with a multi-task objective that combines 8-class persuasion strategy classification and binary jailbreak-intent classification at the turn level. The 8-class taxonomy is grounded in PAP~\citep{zeng2024pap} and Cialdini's principles of influence~\citep{cialdini2001influence}, covering strategies from rapport building and authority appeal to gradual escalation and direct request. The persuasion classification task forces the encoder to learn representations that distinguish between pragmatic strategies, while the intent task anchors these representations to the detection objective. In Stage~2, we aggregate turn-level [CLS] embeddings via mean pooling and train a lightweight MLP for conversation-level binary classification. The full architecture is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}. The design is deliberately simple: the ablation study (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that replacing mean pooling with a GRU yields no improvement, and that even scrambled persuasion labels reduce OOD detection by only 1 percentage point (pp) relative to the full taxonomy, while vanilla DeBERTa without fine-tuning trails by over 70~pp. The fine-tuning process on persuasion-related text, not label accuracy or temporal modeling, is the critical ingredient for cross-attack generalization. This finding parallels domain-adaptive pretraining results~\citep{gururangan2018artifacts}: exposure to in-domain text reshapes the encoder's feature space even when the supervision signal is noisy or coarse. In our setting, multi-task training on persuasion-annotated conversations teaches the encoder to attend to pragmatic cues (implicit requests, escalation markers, rapport-building patterns) that transfer across attack families.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Cross-attack generalization through persuasion-aware fine-tuning.} DisPeD achieves F1 = 1.000 on unseen Deceptive Delight conversations, a +72~pp improvement over vanilla DeBERTa (F1 = 0.284) trained on the same Crescendo data. Ablation experiments show that scrambled strategy labels reduce OOD F1 by only 1~pp, confirming that fine-tuning on persuasion-domain text is the mechanism that bridges the cross-attack generalization gap (Section~\ref{sec:cross_attack}, Section~\ref{sec:ablation}).

  \item \textbf{Interpretable detection through persuasion strategy trajectories.} The 8-class persuasion taxonomy provides native interpretability: different attack types exhibit distinct strategy signatures that security analysts can inspect. Crescendo uses all 8 strategies with gradual escalation across turns; FITD employs only 4 strategies in a commitment-then-escalation pattern. These trajectories explain detection decisions without requiring post-hoc interpretability methods (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).

  \item \textbf{Robustness to adversarial perturbation.} DisPeD maintains zero degradation (0~pp) under adversarial paraphrasing, while vanilla DeBERTa degrades by 11.8~pp and TF-IDF by 1.3~pp. Combined with cross-attack robustness, this confirms that persuasion-aware representations are invariant to both surface variation and attack-type shift (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
\end{itemize}
